notes: Hand-picked, because eBird Status & Trends marks most South African birds as rare (568 of 878) and the automatic cut gives far too few. The list uses GBIF/eBird record counts (November 2026, occurrence.csv) as a ranking signal plus birding knowledge, and covers what a visitor on a normal 2 to 3 week trip meets: Cape Town and the Peninsula (Boulders penguins, Cape Point, Kirstenbosch), the West Coast and Langebaan lagoon, the fynbos and Karoo, the Garden Route and Wilderness, Johannesburg and Pretoria gardens and highveld, the Drakensberg and Wakkerstroom grasslands, KwaZulu-Natal and Zululand (Mkuze, St Lucia, Cape Vidal), Kruger and the Lowveld, and the Kalahari edge, plus the common garden and urban birds. Left out as rare, very local, skulking or needing special trips: vagrants, pelagic seabirds that need a boat (albatrosses, petrels, shearwaters, skuas), most owls and nightjars, most flufftails, pipits and cisticolas that cannot be told apart without a call, the very local indicator species of the Karoo and Namaqualand, and the rarer raptors and bustards. South Africa has 30 endemic-status species in the database. 19 are in the trip because a visitor can find them on the usual route: Cape Weaver, Cape Bulbul, Cape Spurfowl, Grey-winged Francolin and Cape Cormorant of the Cape; Cape Sugarbird, Orange-breasted Sunbird, Cape Siskin, Cape Rock-Thrush and Cape Rockjumper of the fynbos and mountains; Protea Canary; Forest Canary of the Garden Route; Ground Woodpecker, Karoo Lark and Black Korhaan of the dry west; and Drakensberg Rockjumper, Drakensberg Siskin, Drakensberg Prinia and Eastern Long-billed Lark of the eastern escarpment. Dropped as too rare, too local or too hard to find on a normal trip: Knysna Woodpecker, Knysna Warbler, Victorin's Warbler, Fynbos Buttonquail, Red Lark, Rudd's Lark and Botha's Lark (the last two need a guide at Wakkerstroom and often a lot of luck), Yellow-breasted Pipit, Yellow-tufted Pipit, Forest Buzzard, Blue Korhaan and Cape Clapper Lark. Pelagic birds are left out except the Cape Gannet, which breeds on the coast. Blue Swallow is in for the summer visit to the Mpumalanga and KwaZulu-Natal grasslands. Left out for lack of usable photos in the library or because the photos could not be identified with confidence: White-backed Mousebird (whbmou1), Greater Honeyguide (grehon2) and Cape Parrot (bnnpar2). Cape Parrot is a wanted bird (Hogsback and the Karkloof forests); add it back when reviewed photos exist. Several look-alike cisticolas, larks and chats have shaky photo picks, see the owner review list in the report.
